[00:00] Samantha Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for carving time, we'll do a deep lab-style session, hi Maya, how's sh- how's the team doing?
[00:06] Dr. Maya Singh: hey Sam, good — busy but excited, we want to push the tail latency down for our long-convo assistant, last week we saw 95th at 720ms and 99.9 at like 1.8s on qwen-70b in our onprem sim.
[00:19] Ethan Wolfe: ok, that matches some of the numbers we saw reading your perf spreadsheet, one hypothesis is token routing for MoE plus k-v lookups are compounding, also RoPE scale can increase compute for long sequences if not tuned.
[00:31] Tom Barlow: yeah the weird bit is we see spikes when the user resumes long history — kv cache miss pattern looks correlated. sometimes a single request fans out to three GPUs and routing overhead and pci-e copies kick the tail up.
[00:45] Aisha Rahman: quick context — we're running a Dedicated-like onprem cluster, 8x A100-80GB per rack, 100Gbps networking but no customer RDMA in the early sandbox, also we pin model shards with our sharding strategy.
[00:58] Ethan Wolfe: got it, no RDMA increases the PCIe mem copies, that will show up as 99.9 tail. we usually look at two axes: data-path (kv sharding and transfers) and compute-path (kv cache hits, RoPE scaling, quantization overhead).
[01:12] Ravi Patel: can you say a bit more about 'RoPE scaling' — we've seen references to gamma and rope decay, some forum posts call it rope-decay or rope-scale, we're not sure what's safe to change on qwen and mistral.
[01:22] Ethan Wolfe: yeah, sure — so RoPE is positional encoding; when you change the multiplicative scale (sometimes called gamma) you're effectively adjusting how position embeddings attenuate over long contexts. for some model families increasing scale can reduce hallucination over long context but it can also change logits slightly and may require small LR-finetune if you want parity. for inference-only, small fractional changes (e.g., 0.95–1.05) often safe but we test.
[01:43] Dr. Maya Singh: interesting. we saw token drift on a 12k context run where the model started repeating; would that be rope-related or kv-cache stale pointers?
[01:53] Ethan Wolfe: could be both. kv-cache staleness/generation mismatch sometimes looks like repetition; also RoPE mismatch when you concatenate different position spaces or when sequence chunking resets positions.
[02:06] Samantha Ortiz: we prepared a few microbench configs — EV1 is baseline: single-shard KV per GPU with naive batching, EV2 is 4-way KV sharded, EV3 is 8-way, plus toggles for RoPE gamma at .98 and 1.02, and quantize path for 4-bit per-tensor.
[02:22] Tom Barlow: how do you actually shard KV — is it by token-range, by head, or just round-robin across kv shards?
[02:29] Ethan Wolfe: good question, we typically shard KV by key-range using consistent hashing for token affinity, which keeps frequent token keys local to a GPU. alternative is per-attention-head sharding but that raises cross-GPU attention cost. for MoE, routing already fans out; careful interplay needed.
[02:45] [02:45] Ravi Patel: (murmuring) consistent hashing, ok
[02:48] Ethan Wolfe: so for your workload, initial recommendation is 4-way KV sharding with a hot-key map for the top ~2% tokens — those you keep sticky on a primary GPU to avoid routing. that reduces fanout for many requests.
[03:00] Dr. Maya Singh: what's the overhead for maintaining a hot-key sticky map, does it require central coordination?
[03:06] Ethan Wolfe: it's lightweight — a per-node small LRU and a coordinator that periodically aggregates hit counts. you can implement it in the runtime as a shared metadata plane; the cache-management messages are tiny compared to full KV state.
[03:15] [03:15] Aisha: does that change model semantics? like, if a token's key is sticky but we move it later, do outputs change?
[03:20] Ethan Wolfe: outputs should not change semantics; it's a routing/perf optimization. only if your sticky policy causes different GPU-level kernel selection (e.g., quantized vs full) could you get numeric diffs. we try to keep execution deterministic.
[03:33] Samantha Ortiz: quick note — we've uploaded an initial microbenchmark CSV to the shared link: https://redwood.example.com/shared/polaris-kv-microbench it's a small test harness you can pull.
[03:41] Ravi Patel: got it, saw the link, thanks
[03:44] [04:00] Ethan Wolfe: moving to RoPE: we ran a sweep last week on Mistral-family models and found that small gamma downscales reduce long-context attention drift and improved throughput slightly because the decayed attention makes effective sequence compression better for some kernels — results are model dependent.
[04:18] Dr. Maya Singh: throughput improved? why would RoPE change throughput?
[04:21] Ethan Wolfe: two reasons — first, slight decay can reduce effective active window size for softmax numerics which affects attention sparsity heuristics in the runtime, second, kernel selection logic sometimes picks different fused attention kernels if sequence effective length changes. it's subtle.
[04:36] Tom Barlow: about quantization — we want to move to 4-bit for cost reasons but we fear edge-case latency regressions. what tradeoffs have you observed?
[04:45] Ethan Wolfe: 4-bit (per-group quant) gives big memory wins and can increase throughput, but on some kernels the dequantize path can add CPU/GPU copy overhead when combined with KV sharding because we need an unpack step before certain fused attention. on some hardware with fast fused 4-bit kernels we win big; on others the overhead is neutral. run the microbench.
[05:05] [05:05] Aisha Rahman: any rules of thumb for when not to quantize? like large batch low-latency targets?
[05:11] Ethan Wolfe: if your SLO is extreme low-latency for single-request p50/p95 and your kernel stack lacks fused 4-bit attention, stay on 8-bit until you can benchmark. Also MoE routers are sensitive to quant noise — some MoE models need higher precision on routing logits.
[05:26] Dr. Maya Singh: about MoE — we have a small expert-based routing layer for a retrieval component; routing seems to spike network usage dramatically on certain prompts. is there a way to mitigate routing network cost without losing MoE benefit?
[05:39] Ethan Wolfe: yes, a few approaches: top-k routing with per-token affinity (route only high-entropy tokens), combine MoE with local-expert caching — keep hot experts co-located with hot keys, and apply routing budgets per-request so only N tokens can fan out. this reduces network blowup.
[05:55] [06:00] Ravi Patel: how do you measure routing cost in the runtime? is there a metric we can track in the console?
[06:05] Samantha Ortiz: yes, Redwood Console exposes per-token fanout, cross-GPU bytes, and router latency. we can add a dashboard tile for your account showing router bytes by endpoint.
[06:12] Tom Barlow: we don't have RDMA in the sandbox — how much will that hurt for cross-GPU KV transfers?
[06:18] Ethan Wolfe: without RDMA you pay PCIe and kernel copy overhead which shows up in the 99.9 tail. RDMA lowers CPU involvement and can drop tail significantly for big KV transfers. In absence of RDMA we recommend smaller sharded transfers and more cache locality (hot keys sticky).
[06:33] Priya Menon (joined): sorry for the late hop in, quick Q — on the sharding strategies, do you have an automated rebalancer for hotspot mitigation?
[06:40] Ethan Wolfe: yes, we use a light-weight rebalance policy: measure key hit rates per epoch, migrate top-k hotspots gradually during low-load windows, and use background streaming (throttle-copy) to avoid tail impact.
[06:53] Dr. Maya Singh: from a correctness lens, does background migration risk missing keys during migration?
[06:58] Ethan Wolfe: we serve dual-read during handoff (read from both source and dest) then atomically switch the metadata pointer; writes route to both until cutover completes. that slightly increases write cost during migration window but avoids misses.
[07:13] Samantha Ortiz: (brief) important to note — for onprem Dedicated we can enable migration windows during your low traffic period; we can script it in the deployment plan.
[07:21] [07:30] Aisha Rahman: switching to batching — we saw compound latency under variable request sizes. is adaptive batch sizing stable for low p50 targets?
[07:37] Ethan Wolfe: adaptive batching can achieve a good balance: predict per-request token-length and form batches that honor a max latency horizon. we use headroom buckets and can preemptively flush if tail grows. there is a tradeoff: slightly higher p50 for much lower 99.9.
[07:52] Ravi Patel: can we do a hybrid approach: small immediate fast-path for single-turn queries, and a background batch for long-history expansions?
[07:58] Ethan Wolfe: absolutely — we implement dual queues: a hot fast-path with very small max batch, and a slow-path that aggregates long history. prefix caching helps: if prefix is cached we often do a single quick lookup.
[08:11] Dr. Maya Singh: any specific kernel flags we should toggle for Qwen-70B to favor latency vs throughput?
[08:17] Ethan Wolfe: on qwen we often prefer fused attention with streaming enabled for latency — disable large-block GEMMs that expect huge batches. also enable kv-store prefetch and reduce KV read-ahead window for low-latency mode. we'll send a config snippet.
[08:30] Samantha Ortiz: note: Priya will drop a config gist after the call — it's in the follow-ups.
[08:36] [08:48] Tom Barlow: security question — if we implement hot-key sticky mapping, are there leakage concerns? like some user tokens being pinned arbitrarily?
[08:56] Ethan Wolfe: the mapping is purely runtime metadata; it doesn't change persistence or logs. if compliance needs per-tenant separation we can ensure sticky maps are namespaced per-tenant and enforce RBAC on map management.
[09:08] Dr. Maya Singh: let's talk numbers — what improvement should we expect with 4-way KV + hot-key sticky + adaptive batching?
[09:15] Ethan Wolfe: from our lab on similar workloads we saw 95th reduce by ~30–45% and 99.9 by ~40–60% depending on RDMA presence. in your RDMA-less sandbox you should still expect a ~25–35% reduction if hot keys are skewed as you described.
[09:32] Ravi Patel: that would be huge.
[09:34] [09:45] Ethan Wolfe: also note RoPE gamma tuning reduced repetition and allowed us to reduce effective active window, which indirectly helped batch packing and kernel selection. but we always validate on held-out prompts.
[09:56] Aisha Rahman: any failure modes to watch out for when we change RoPE?
[10:01] Ethan Wolfe: if you change gamma too aggressively you can shift token distribution and cause minor output drift; run a regression eval and human spot-check for a small sample. avoid large changes mid-production.
[10:12] Samantha Ortiz: ok, let's walk the microbench plan — Ethan, can you outline the experiments?
[10:17] Ethan Wolfe: sure: 1) baseline single-shard KV, naive batching, default RoPE; 2) 4-way KV sharded + hot-key sticky; 3) 8-way KV; 4) repeat 2 & 3 with RoPE gamma 0.98 and 1.02; 5) 4-bit quant path toggles on top of best sharding; measure p50/p95/p99/p99.9, cross-gpu bytes, router fanout, and kernel selection logs. we'll run traffic shapes: short-chat, long-chat, mixed.
[10:45] Tom Barlow: how long will each experiment take? we want to minimize disruption.
[10:49] Ethan Wolfe: each run can be done in 20–30 minutes per traffic shape; the whole sweep about 5 hours if you run serially. we can parallelize across nodes for faster turnaround.
[10:59] [11:10] Dr. Maya Singh: for regression criteria, what thresholds should we set to accept a change to production?
[11:16] Ethan Wolfe: recommend: p50 no worse than +5% and p95 no worse than +10% for any config; 99.9 must improve or at least not regress. quality checks: perplexity delta < 0.5% and spot-checked hallucination rate not increased.
[11:35] Priya Menon: also add a short A/B canary: route 5% traffic to the config and monitor for 24–48h. Redwood console can automate rollback if metrics breach.
[11:45] Samantha Ortiz: ok, logistics — we'll push Ethan's microbench scripts and a config bundle. we'll also need Ravi's traces.
[11:53] Ravi Patel: I'll export traces after this call and upload to your shared link.
[11:57] [12:05] Aisha Rahman: final note — we have an internal compliance ask: we need KMS integration and audit logs for any onprem key operations before we turn on dedicated. is Redwood's private packaging supporting HSM/KMS hooks?
[12:16] Samantha Ortiz: yes, Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs; I'll attach the security checklist and SOC2 artifacts in the follow-up email.
[12:25] Dr. Maya Singh: great. any competitive notes — we also chatted with one of the big vendors, they recommended batching-only, but they don't have the kv sharding story.
[12:33] Ethan Wolfe: that's a common pattern — batching helps but doesn't address KV/KV-fanout for MoE. our hybrid approach aims to combine both.
